workflows.building: Building a new character: pick archetype and powersets, say what you will run (Content) and what you are there to do (Role), then let Solve design the build. Tune afterward.
workflows.updating: Updating a character you already have: import it (from the game or from Mids Reborn), let the tool evaluate it, then Solve with Preserve or Locks so your real investments are kept.
workflows.tweaking: Tweaking with the optimizer: state a goal or custom targets, press Solve, and read the before-and-after. The tool re-slots everything you have not locked, in about a second.
workflows.manual: Changing things by hand: the Stats page is the workbench. Click any enhancement to see what it is worth, swap or remove it with every option priced, and undo anything.

loop: Say what you want more of - a goal in the Build Assistant, or exact numbers in Custom targets.
Press Solve. It re-slots every earned slot toward that goal and shows a before-and-after.
Tune one piece at a time on the Stats page, where every change is priced and undoable.
Change powers last - picks reshape the whole build, so settle slotting questions first.

topics.what: Runs the optimizer over your build: every earned slot is re-slotted toward your goal, and the result comes back as a before-and-after report naming each number that moved.
topics.how: It searches real slotting choices under the game's actual math (to-hit, defense, resistance, endurance, recharge, enhancement diversification) and stops when no single change improves the build. Powers you picked are left alone; locked powers are untouched down to the enhancement.
topics.why: Hand-slotting 67 slots against interacting caps and set bonuses is the hardest part of build planning. The tool does that part; you keep the decisions.
topics.where: Step 2 of the loop. State a goal first, Solve, then tune the result on Stats.
go: Show me the workflow in the tour

topics.what: The panel where you say what you want more of - in plain words or with sliders - and press Solve.
topics.how: Your words become targets (defense types, recharge, endurance, damage), and the optimizer chases them. It never touches the powers you picked and never moves a locked enhancement. It cannot yet be asked for one specific SET by name; slot that piece by hand, lock the power, and Solve builds around it.
topics.why: So improving an existing build is one sentence and one click instead of an evening of slot shuffling.
topics.where: Steps 1 and 2 of the loop, on Powers & Slots.

topics.what: Exact numbers you want the build to reach - for example 45% melee defense, or a recharge figure.
topics.how: Your stated targets take priority at both layers: which powers are proposed and how slots are placed. The tool states in numbers what each target costs elsewhere, and refuses only the genuinely unreachable - with the reason and a remedy, never silently.
topics.why: Presets fit most people; custom targets exist for the player who knows exactly what they are building toward.
topics.where: Step 1 of the loop, feeding Solve.

topics.what: After a solve, a list comparing what you asked for against what the build reached.
topics.how: A row that fell short also names which unpicked powers on your character would help and roughly how much each would add. If nothing on your character supplies a stat, it says so plainly.
topics.why: A goal you cannot reach is worth knowing about rather than chasing.
topics.where: Read it right after Solve, before you start tuning.

topics.what: The hands-on half of the tool: every number in your build, broken down to the powers and enhancements making it, and editable one piece at a time.
topics.how: Click a stat to see its contributors. Click any enhancement in the miniature build to see exactly what it is worth. Swap or remove it right there; every change reports a before-and-after and hands you an Undo.
topics.why: The Build Assistant is the global tool; Stats is where you change one thing and watch the numbers move. Both exist because some decisions are yours, not the optimizer's.
topics.where: Step 3 of the loop: tune here after Solve, before changing powers.

topics.what: Click any enhancement on the Stats page and a panel lists every number that one piece is buying you, set bonuses included.
topics.how: It is measured, not estimated: the tool rebuilds your character without that piece and compares. That is why pulling one Defense/Endurance piece can show a max-HP cost - it dropped a whole set tier a shortcut would have missed.
topics.why: To find the piece you can most afford to give up, with the least impact on the build.
topics.where: The heart of manual tweaking on Stats.

topics.what: The enhancement picker, with every legal replacement priced before you commit.
topics.how: Each candidate shows what it would do to the stat you are working on, plus your set-bonus count. It greys out what the game refuses: a unique you already hold elsewhere (naming the power holding it), a duplicate piece in the same power. On an optimizer-built build most swaps on the optimized stat read as a loss - that is honest: the solver already put the best piece there.
topics.why: So a swap is an informed trade, not a surprise.
topics.where: Manual tweaking on Stats, or anywhere you open a slot.

topics.what: Every edit you make reports what it changed - the real before and after on every number that moved - and offers an Undo.
topics.how: The report covers any change from any surface, not just the Stats panel. Opening a character is not an edit and never fills the undo history.
topics.why: Fearless experimentation: you can always see what a change did and take it back.
topics.where: Everywhere you edit, throughout tweaking and manual work.

topics.what: The padlock on every power card: closed means the optimizer may not touch that power at all.
topics.how: A locked power comes out of a re-solve exactly as you left it, down to the individual enhancements - and an empty slot inside it stays empty (the tool tells you when that happened). Locks are saved with the character.
topics.why: For decisions you have already made: sets you own in game and will not re-buy, a favourite proc, or a what-if with part of the build held fixed. A poorly slotted lock honestly limits what the rest can reach.
topics.where: Set locks before Solve, whenever your build carries investments to protect.
go: Show me a power card in the tour

topics.what: A solve mode that keeps the sets you have already invested in and only re-slots generic enhancements and empty slots.
topics.how: Set pieces stay put; the optimizer works in the space that is left. Locks are the scalpel for specific powers; preserve is the broad stroke for a whole build.
topics.why: Imported characters usually carry real in-game investments. A plan that assumes you will re-buy everything is not a plan.
topics.where: The updating workflow: import, then Solve with preserve on (it is the default for imports).

topics.what: One door, two routes: a character you actually play (from the game itself), or a planned build from Mids Reborn (.mbd).
topics.how: For a played character: type /build_save_file in game, then let the tool find your Homecoming saves itself - unusual install location? Tell it your game folder once and it remembers. For a planned build: load the .mbd file Mids saves. Either way the tool evaluates the build first and can optimize from there.
topics.why: Most players arrive with a character, not a blank slate.
topics.where: The front door of the updating workflow. Character menu, Import a build.

topics.what: The game's own chat command that writes your current character's build to a text file.
topics.how: Type it in game once per character. The file lands under your Homecoming accounts folder, and the tool's import search finds it there - it reports which folders it searched, so a miss tells you what to fix.
topics.why: It is the only route that captures the character you really play, slotting and all.
topics.where: First step of importing a played character.

topics.what: The community's standard build planner. Hero Companion imports and exports its .mbd files, both directions.
topics.how: The round trip is verified piece for piece: every power returns, every slot keeps its exact piece, and the numbers do not move. Export lives in the Character menu.
topics.why: Your builds are yours. If you use this tool, you have every reason to keep using Mids too - the data it ships comes from the Mids team's database.
topics.where: Both ends of the updating workflow: import at the start, export when you are done.

topics.what: The dropdown that says what you actually run: general play, task forces, incarnate trials, fire farms, PvP.
topics.how: It sets what the build must survive and deliver - the scenario the optimizer scores against. Endgame content also unlocks Hamidon Origin proposals.
topics.why: A farm build and a trial build are different answers. The tool needs to know the question.
topics.where: One of the two most important choices, made at building time and changeable any time.

aliases: what you are there to do
topics.what: What you are there to do on a team: damage, tank, buff/debuff support, control, healing - or a Split role naming several jobs and how much of each.
topics.how: The optimizer maximizes your role output, not a generic score. A support character is scored on how much its debuffs and buffs change fights (magnitude times uptime), not on its own survival.
topics.why: The game is role-based, and a support build slotted like a damage build is noticed by nobody. Off-role is warned about, never blocked - the choice stays yours.
topics.where: Beside Content at building time; every role states the real targets it holds.
go: Show me the Split role in the tour
Show me role output in the tour

topics.what: The four-step loop at the top of Powers & Slots: say what you want, Solve, tune on Stats, change powers last.
topics.how: Each step links to the surface that does it. The guided tour teaches the same order and what each step hands back.
topics.why: The most useful criticism this tool ever received was that it offered many choices and no obvious order. This is the order.
topics.where: It IS the workflow - everything else in this help hangs off one of its steps.

topics.what: The fifth power category, opening at level 35. Separate from your four power pools and does not count against them.
topics.how: Switching your epic offers to finish the job: take the new pool's powers into the freed seats and re-slot toward your goal in one action - or switch and pick them yourself. Epic powers follow the same tier prerequisites as pools.
topics.why: Changing an epic used to strand you with empty seats and a manual rebuild. Now it is one decision.
topics.where: A power-level change - step 4 of the loop, after slotting questions are settled.

topics.what: The shared power menus (Fighting, Leadership, Speed, and the rest). The game allows at most four per build.
topics.how: The rules come from the game's own files: four pools maximum, the epic does not count against them, only one origin-themed pool (Sorcery, Experimentation, Force of Will) per build, and tier prerequisites - a tier-3 power needs one other power from its pool, tiers 4 and 5 need two.
topics.why: The tool only ever offers what the game would let you take; anything greyed out tells you why.
topics.where: Building and manual power changes - the rules apply everywhere picks happen.

topics.what: How many other powers from its own pool a power requires before the game lets you take it.
topics.how: Read from the game's own rules, power by power: most travel powers need nothing, Weave or Vengeance need two others from their pool. The picker greys out what you cannot take yet and says why.
topics.why: The tool proposing a build the game refuses would be worse than no tool. Every certified build is checked against these rules.
topics.where: Enforced silently through building and manual picks.

topics.what: Extra stats a build earns for slotting several pieces of the same enhancement set in one power.
topics.how: Each additional piece of a set unlocks the next bonus tier. Bonuses are counted per distinct piece and survive exemplaring while you are within 3 levels of the piece. The same bonus value counts at most five times across a build - the rule of five.
topics.why: Set bonuses are where endgame defense and recharge really come from; the optimizer's whole search is largely about them.
topics.where: Reference - consulted constantly while tweaking and swapping.

topics.what: The game counts any identical set-bonus value at most five times across your whole build.
topics.how: A sixth copy of the same bonus adds nothing: six 7.5% Luck of the Gambler recharge pieces pay 37.5%, not 45%. The tool counts it the game's way, and the per-enhancement worth panel shows when a piece's bonus is already dead under the cap.
topics.why: It is the game's rule, and builds that ignore it waste slots.
topics.where: Reference, enforced in every solve and every swap price.

topics.what: Pieces the game allows once per build - many procs and special IOs.
topics.how: The picker greys out a unique you already hold and names the power holding it. Luck of the Gambler's Defense/Global Recharge is deliberately still offered repeatedly, because the game does allow that one many times.
topics.why: Refusing what the game refuses, before it becomes an error later.
topics.where: Reference, enforced in the picker and the validator.

topics.what: The game's diminishing returns on stacking the same enhancement aspect in one power.
topics.how: Past thresholds, each further point of the same aspect is worth less - a third damage SO adds far less than the first. The tool prices every piece post-ED, which is why the measured worth of a piece is not its label value.
topics.why: ED is why 'just slot six damage' stopped being a build strategy in 2005, and why measured worth beats reading the label.
topics.where: Reference, baked into every number the tool shows.

topics.what: 45% defense - the point where most incoming attacks have reached their floor chance to hit you.
topics.how: Each stat bar marks the number that matters: 45% for defense. Points past the line are wasted against ordinary enemies, and the optimizer knows it.
topics.why: The single most important number in survival building.
topics.where: Reference - the line on every defense bar.

topics.what: The most resistance the game will count for your archetype: 90% for Tankers and Brutes, 85% for Kheldians and the Arachnos archetypes, 75% for everyone else.
topics.how: The bar marks your archetype's cap; past it the game stops counting, and the optimizer stops paying for it.
topics.why: Spending slots past a cap is the classic invisible waste.
topics.where: Reference - the line on every resistance bar.

topics.what: The '⚔ N%' figure on a defense row: what a Hide-style defense drops to the moment you attack.
topics.how: When suppression applies, the row shows both numbers - resting and in-combat. The honest number rides alongside; it never replaces the other.
topics.why: The in-combat figure is what you have when it matters; plan around it.
topics.where: Reference, on the Stats bars.

topics.what: Enhancements with a chance to fire an effect - bonus damage, a heal, endurance - instead of boosting the power's own numbers.
topics.how: Priced by the game's per-power proc math (recharge and area drive the chance). When the optimizer trades set pieces for procs, the enhancement card says what was traded and why. Procs keep firing at any exemplar level, which is why proc-heavy builds exemplar well.
topics.why: Procs are the endgame's damage currency, and the trade against set bonuses is a real decision the tool makes visible.
topics.where: Reference; the tour's 'Why these enhancements' step shows the trade note.
go: Show me the proc trade in the tour

topics.what: Enhancements carrying two or three aspects in one slot - more raw enhancement per slot than any set piece, but no set bonuses.
topics.how: For endgame content (incarnate trials, farms) the optimizer may propose them where they genuinely beat a set piece; every HO it places says where it comes from (Hamidon raids or merit conversion). You can slot them by hand anywhere.
topics.why: In half the slots, three HOs can match a six-piece set's enhancement - the trade is bonuses for ceiling.
topics.where: Reference; appears in endgame solves.
go: Show me HOs in the tour

topics.what: Set pieces whose level follows your character instead of being fixed.
topics.how: In the exemplar view, attuned pieces keep paying set bonuses down to the set's minimum level minus 3. The exemplar banner shows the fully-attuned counterfactual: what going attuned would save you at your chosen level.
topics.why: The difference between a build that works at 50 and one that works on every task force.
topics.where: Reference; decisive in the exemplar view.

topics.what: Enhancement boosters push a piece up to +5 levels of value.
topics.how: Shown as display preview only. Builds are never scored or certified on boosted values - certification is clean, and boosting is a later upgrade you apply in game.
topics.why: Scoring boosted values would let the plan promise numbers your wallet has not paid for yet.
topics.where: Reference; a display option, never an assumption.

topics.what: Set the level a task force will drop you to, and the whole app shows that truth: powers that switch off, set bonuses that go dead, what attuned pieces would save.
topics.how: The game's rules, applied per piece: powers earned more than 5 levels above the cap switch off (inherents, accolades and temps keep working); set bonuses pay while you are within 3 levels of the piece and survive losing the host power; purple, PvP, Winter and archetype sets follow you all the way down; procs keep firing; incarnates stop below 45. It can even solve FOR that level if you ask.
topics.why: Half the game happens exemplared. A build that only works at 50 is half a build.
topics.where: A view for tweaking - it never changes what is saved or solved unless you ask for the exemplar solve.

topics.what: A level-by-level walk from 1 to 50 on the real Homecoming schedule: every pick, every slot, respec trials, cost-smart enhancement advice per stretch.
topics.how: Powers on the game's own grant ladder, pools at 4, epics at 35. Kheldians follow their own rules (inherent flight, forms, no epic). Arachnos Soldiers and Widows get the honest two-phase career with the level-24 respec and the full re-place order. Deviate freely - it re-fits around your actual choices.
topics.why: The game's leveling rules are real constraints, and a plan that ignores them cannot be followed.
topics.where: The building workflow for from-scratch characters; also carries the zones, badges and Flashback references.

topics.what: The four-way switch: Hero, Vigilante, Rogue, Villain. It reskins the app and sets which side's accolades count.
topics.how: Your build scores the same either way - the game counts Vigilante as hero-side and Rogue as villain-side. Off-side accolades stay remembered, grey out, and count zero until you switch back, exactly as the game gates them. The Leveling Guide's own switch is a separate PREVIEW of other routes and resets when you leave.
topics.why: What you see should match the character you play, without ever moving a number it should not.
topics.where: Reference; set it once in the banner.

topics.what: Earned account powers (Atlas Medallion, Task Force Commander and the rest) that carry real stats.
topics.how: Tick the ones your character holds in the Accolades panel; they join your totals. They are alignment-gated the way the game gates them: an off-side accolade is held but dormant.
topics.why: Accolades are real HP and endurance; a plan without them is planning a weaker character than you own.
topics.where: Reference; the panel lives under the powers wall.

topics.what: The endgame power tier. The End-game plan panel recommends slots per role and content.
topics.how: Included in totals when you say so; the exemplar view switches them off below level 45, as the game does.
topics.why: Endgame builds are judged with incarnates in play; hiding them would misprice trial builds.
topics.where: Reference; the End-game plan fold on Powers & Slots.

topics.what: The best certified build for an archetype + powersets + content combination. Champions ship with the app and give the optimizer its head start.
topics.how: Each is produced by long convergence runs, checked to be buildable in game exactly as shown, and stamped with the model version that certified it. Think your build beats one? Submit it as a candidate from the Help menu; genuine wins ship in a future update with credit.
topics.why: The learning loop: what the search proved best becomes what autopick proposes, and the community can beat it.
topics.where: Reference; champions power the 'Start a new character' proposals.

topics.what: The stamp saying which generation of scoring physics produced a number; the data version stamps which game database it ran against.
topics.how: Scores are only compared apples to apples. When the model improves (v44 today), shipped champion scores are re-certified under it, and your build's numbers can move in both directions - the pricing getting closer to the game, not your build changing.
topics.why: A number without its model version is a number you cannot trust across updates.
topics.where: Reference; shown in About and on every certified build.

topics.what: Some real mechanics are shown but not scored, on purpose, and the app says so where they appear.
topics.how: Mez protection is in the data and on screen but needs a decision about how often content mezzes you before it can move a score. Criticals use the game's lower stated chance (the boss-rank premium needs an enemy-rank mix). Domination's magnitude half is ambiguous in the game's files, so only its duration is priced.
topics.why: Understatement over guesswork. A number the tool cannot ground in the game's own files does not get invented.
topics.where: Reference; the Stats page marks each mechanic counted, shown only, or not modeled.

topics.what: Answers 'how do I get this IO cheaply?': which piece to buy or craft, which converters to use, and the cost.
topics.how: Concrete cheapest path per enhancement, honoring the game's conversion rules - conversions cannot jump from cheap pools into purples, and the paths never pretend otherwise.
topics.why: The market is half the endgame; a plan you cannot afford is a poster.
topics.where: Reference slab on Powers & Slots.

topics.what: Paste your drops (recipes included) and each gets a verdict: keep for your build, craft-then-convert for profit, or just sell.
topics.how: It knows your build, so 'keep' means genuinely useful to this character - not generically valuable.
topics.why: Turning play sessions into build progress without a spreadsheet.
topics.where: Reference slab on Powers & Slots.

topics.what: Optional, off by default: reads the game's chat logs you point it at, to track your characters' progress and (separately opt-in) public recruitment activity.
topics.how: Strictly local unless you switch sharing on yourself, which puts the terms in front of you first. Structured facts only, never general conversation. Both switches live on the Logging tab and turn off from the same place they turn on.
topics.why: Some players want their play reflected in the tool; nobody gets it without asking.
topics.where: The Logging tab, outside the build loop entirely.

topics.what: All 390 exploration badges, listed under their zones, with directions and what each commemorates.
topics.how: Click a badge name and the tool copies a /thumbtack command with its coordinates - the command the game client registers for placing a minimap marker. Paste it in the chat box while in that zone. (Whether the marker lands exactly where expected is still unconfirmed in game.)
topics.why: Finding one badge used to cost an expand and a read-down per zone.
topics.where: The Leveling Guide's zones and badges catalogue.

topics.what: Characters save locally - plan, progress, locks, targets, everything - and auto-save runs in the background.
topics.how: Named characters update automatically; the Continue list shows each save's real state ('In progress, N of 24 picks'). Nothing ever leaves your machine.
topics.why: Resume exactly where you left off, always.
topics.where: Reference; the Character menu.

topics.what: A step-by-step walk of every surface, on a safe example build - it never touches your character.
topics.how: Pick a chapter or take the whole thing; your spot can be saved and resumed. Question-mark buttons around the app deep-link to the exact step explaining that control.
topics.why: The fastest way to learn the tool is being shown, in place.
topics.where: Help menu, Guided tour. It teaches the same four-step loop this help describes.
